speaker_role: independent counselor (Jason Fleury, certified financial planner and self-described 'college planning specialist,' not an admissions officer)
commercial_incentive: yes; podcast for a paid financial/college-planning practice, plugs the firm's website and email at the end
key_insights: Recommends checking each target college's Common Data Set to see whether that specific school weights rigor or GPA more heavily, rather than assuming a universal rule
If a school's data shows GPA weighted more heavily than rigor, advises protecting GPA rather than adding AP/dual-enrollment courses that risk lowering it

Argues it is easier to explain why a student didn't overload on AP courses than to explain a lower-than-expected GPA, and a GPA shortfall can disqualify a student from scholarships even with a strong overall application
States colleges are more flexible on rigor when a student's schedule is constrained by heavy extracurricular time commitments (band, sports, caregiving, jobs)
Notes honors courses, not just AP/IB/dual enrollment, count as rigor too, which matters for smaller or private schools with limited AP offerings
Claims a GPA that narrowly misses a scholarship cutoff due to AP-related grade dips can cost a family $60,000-$100,000 in lost scholarship money over four years
specific_numbers_or_facts: Presenter claims lost-scholarship gaps from missed GPA cutoffs can total $60,000-$100,000 over 4 years (unsourced, from presenter's client experience)
notable_or_distinctive: unusually assertive in prioritizing GPA protection over rigor-stacking as a default rule ('10 out of 10 times' prefers a higher GPA over more rigor with a middling GPA), more direct than the balanced framing typical elsewhere
reliability_notes: presenter is a financial planner, not an admissions professional; dollar-loss figures are anecdotal client-experience claims rather than data, though the underlying Common-Data-Set strategy is sound
